14-5.title: If your card is used fraudulently, report and freeze it first; your liability depends on how fast you report
14-5.inPlainWords: The RBI's 2017 circular on unauthorised electronic transactions limits your liability if you report at once: zero liability where the fraud is due to a third party and you report within three working days. The bank must credit the amount within 10 working days. Report to the bank and on 1930, and keep the acknowledgement.
14-5.benefit: The RBI circular sets a zero-liability rule for a third-party breach reported within three working days, and limited liability for a delay. The bank must resolve the complaint within 90 days. The IT Act and the BNS cover the fraud. A chargeback is separate from the bank's liability. A bank cannot make you pay for its own security failure.
14-5.cost: No cost. Report on the bank's hotline and in writing, then on 1930.
14-5.caveats: A delay can shift part of the liability to you. Do not share the OTP or PIN, even with a caller who claims to be from the bank. Keep the card blocked until the investigation ends.
14-5.sources: Reserve Bank of India, customer protection circular on unauthorised electronic transactions. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

14-11.title: Audit the SIM cards and bank accounts linked to your identity once a year
14-11.inPlainWords: India limits the number of SIM cards a person may hold. Use the Sanchar Saathi or TAFCOP portal to see the mobile connections in your name and report an unknown one. Check your credit report for a loan or card you did not apply for, and close an unused account. An unknown SIM can be used for OTP fraud.
14-11.benefit: The Department of Telecommunications' TAFCOP lets you check the mobile connections issued against your ID and report the unauthorised ones. The RBI's KYC rules require the bank to verify the customer. A credit bureau report shows a loan or card in your name. The Aadhaar Act restricts the use of Aadhaar. The BNS and the IT Act cover identity theft.
14-11.cost: No cost. The TAFCOP check is free, and the annual credit report is free.
14-11.caveats: A family member may have used your ID for a SIM; ask before reporting. A closed account can still show for a month. Do not share an OTP with anyone who offers to 'check' your SIM.
14-11.sources: Department of Telecommunications, Sanchar Saathi. <https://sancharsaathi.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; TransUnion CIBIL. <https://www.cibil.com/>; Aadhaar Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

14-7.title: Don't tap “Allow all” just to use an app: consent must be specific and informed, and you can refuse the permissions the app does not need
14-7.cost: No cost involved. The hard part is resisting the urge to tap “Allow all”.
14-7.inPlainWords: An app asks for a bundle of permissions at once, and “Allow all” is a single tap that hands over contacts, location, microphone and storage together. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, and limited to the personal data necessary for the purpose the app has told you about. A map app can ask for location; a torch app has no business asking for your contacts. You can install the app, refuse the extras, and withdraw consent later as easily as you gave it.
14-7.benefit: Section 6(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 defines consent as a free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous agreement, given by a clear affirmative action, to the processing of personal data for a specified purpose, limited to the data necessary for that purpose. Section 5 requires the company to give you notice of the data and the purpose before it asks for consent. Sections 6(4) and 6(5) require withdrawing consent to be as easy as giving it. India's Act does not contain an express right to refuse consent and still receive the service; that protection exists in the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, not here. What you can rely on is purpose limitation, the notice, and the phone's own permission controls.
14-7.caveats: The deciding factor is simple: is this data actually necessary for the service? Location is necessary for a map; a contact list is not necessary for a torch. After installing an app, open the phone's app-permission settings and turn off anything the app does not need; grant a permission when you actually use it, and prefer “only this time” to “while using the app”. If an app will not work unless you hand over data that is plainly unrelated to what it does, that is a reason to use another app, and you can complain to the Data Protection Board of India, which the Act sets up to hear such complaints.
14-7.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, customer protection. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>

14-8.title: You can ask a company to show you, correct and erase your personal data — and complain to the Data Protection Board if it refuses
14-8.cost: No cost to make the request. If the company drags its feet, the next step is a complaint to the Data Protection Board of India, which is free; a civil suit for damages is a separate, slow and expensive route.
14-8.inPlainWords: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 you can ask a company what personal data it holds about you and get a summary, ask for correction or erasure, complain about how it handled your data, and nominate someone to exercise these rights if you die or become incapacitated. Deactivating an account and erasing the data are two separate actions, so after you close the account, ask for erasure separately. If the company refuses or ignores you, you can complain to the Data Protection Board of India.
14-8.benefit: The Act gives four rights. Section 11 lets you ask for a summary of the personal data a Data Fiduciary holds about you, the identity of the fiduciaries it has shared it with, and a description of the data. Section 12 gives you correction, completion and updating, and erasure where the purpose has been served and there is no legal duty to keep it. Section 13 gives you a grievance-redressal route, and the company must answer. Section 14 lets you nominate someone to exercise your rights if you die or become incapacitated. The Data Protection Board of India, set up under section 18, hears complaints and can impose penalties.
14-8.caveats: The right to erasure stops where another law requires retention: a bank keeps KYC records under the RBI's master directions, a company keeps tax and company-law records, and an investigation can put a hold on data. Deactivating an account is not the same as erasing the data, so ask for both, in writing. Before you switch phones or sell a device, log out of every account, unlink them and factory-reset the handset. The Act gives you a complaint route and penalties, not compensation; a claim for money would need a separate civil suit. The law cannot retrieve data that has already leaked.
14-8.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC Master Direction. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>

14-9.title: You are not obliged to use facial recognition: ask for a password, an OTP, a card or an in-person check instead
14-9.cost: No cost involved. When you are asked for a face scan, ask what other verification methods are available. The challenge is voicing the question on the spot.
14-9.inPlainWords: A face scan is convenient, but it is rarely the only way to prove who you are. India has no facial-recognition-specific statute of the kind that would stop a private operator from making it the only option. What India does have is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which covers biometric data like any other personal data: it needs your free, specific, informed consent, a notice of the purpose, and no more data than the purpose requires. So you can decline, ask for an alternative, and withdraw consent later.
14-9.benefit: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has no special regime for faces; the same rules apply to biometric data. Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, and limited to what is necessary (section 6). The company must give you notice of what it will collect and why (section 5), and must let you withdraw consent as easily as you gave it. For a government body, Aadhaar authentication is voluntary: the Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2018) held that Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for a service without legal backing, and the Aadhaar Act, 2016 requires consent and provides for alternative means of identification. For banks, the RBI's KYC Master Direction recognises video-based customer identification with the customer's consent, alongside branch and other modes.
14-9.caveats: Common requests come from apartment gates, gyms, hotels and rental platforms. When you are told “the system only does face recognition”, ask for the alternative and put the request in writing; a card, a PIN, an OTP or a photo-ID check usually exists. India has no rule that bans cameras in changing rooms, but filming a person in a private space without consent is the offence of voyeurism under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the data protection Act applies to whatever is captured. Financial and government services may have their own rules. Unlike a password, a face cannot be changed after a leak, so it deserves more caution. Your rights to see and erase the data are covered in item 8.
14-9.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Aadhaar Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Unique Identification Authority of India. <https://uidai.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC Master Direction. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>

14-12.title: Before you give up a mobile number, move every account off it — and port the number instead if you can
14-12.cost: No cost apart from the operator's porting charge. Migrating accounts takes an hour or two, and updating the number registered with your bank is done in the banking app or at the branch. The difficulty is remembering the rarely used services.
14-12.inPlainWords: A disconnected mobile number goes back into the operator's pool and is eventually allotted to someone else. Any account still linked to that number can then be unlocked with a one-time password sent by SMS to the new owner. So before you surrender a number, move your bank, UPI, email, social and government accounts to the new number; India has no single “unbind everything” service, so this is done provider by provider. If you are only changing operator or circle, port the number instead, under mobile number portability, and keep every linkage intact.
14-12.benefit: India's mobile number portability regime, run under the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India's portability regulations, lets you keep the number when you change operator or circle, which avoids the problem entirely for most people. The Department of Telecommunications' Sanchar Saathi portal lets you see the connections issued in your name and report one you do not recognise. There is no Indian equivalent of the single national unbinding service that some countries run: each bank, wallet, email provider and social platform has its own change-of-number or account-closure route, and the RBI's KYC master directions require your bank to keep the registered mobile number current. Do the accounts that can move money first.
14-12.caveats: Start with the accounts that can move money — bank, UPI, cards, demat, insurance — and only then the social and shopping accounts. Keep the old number alive on the cheapest plan for one to two months so that a forgotten verification code still reaches you, and forward calls if the operator allows it. Check the connections in your name on Sanchar Saathi before you close anything. If a number is already disconnected, the operator cannot recover the SMS and you will have to prove your identity to each provider another way, which is slow. Managing unauthorised device logins is covered in Chapter 14, Rule 6; wiping an old phone before selling it is covered in Rule 8.
